questions.learningObjective: Explain what survives of an installation once it is dismantled.

options.text: The surviving records fix the work's appearance and condition, since the objects are dispersed
The crates are the finished work, so the photographs are only supporting material
options.misconception: mistakes the packing cases for the artwork

questions.explanation: When an installation is dismantled, the crates, fittings and photographs become the evidence of what was made and how it was installed. Those records let a viewer reconstruct the work even though the components are scattered.

questions.topic: A print and its plate set side by side
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a printing matrix from the impression pulled from it.
questions.stem: A file note lists a print and the copper plate beside it: the plate shows the incised lines filled with ink, while the print shows those lines as a clean image.

options.text: The plate and the print are two impressions made at different times from one block
options.misconception: calls the matrix an impression

options.text: The plate is the working matrix and the print is the record of the image pulled from it
The print is the matrix, and the plate is a later copy kept for reference
options.misconception: reverses matrix and impression

options.text: Both are impressions, the plate simply being printed with a heavier ink
options.misconception: thinks the plate was pulled like a print

questions.explanation: The plate is the matrix: ink sits in its cut lines and transfers to paper under pressure, so it records the making process rather than the finished picture. The print is the impression.
questions.hint: One is the tool, one is the result.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ink rolled across a drawn stone
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a lithographic stone must be re-inked before every impression.
questions.stem: A file note asks why the printer must roll fresh ink onto the stone before each impression instead of reusing the first coat.

answer.exemplar: Lithographic ink is a heavy, oily film that sits on the surface of the stone rather than sinking into it, and every pull of the paper takes most of that film away with it. If the stone were not re-inked, the second impression would carry a thinner and patchier film than the first, and the printed image would lose both its density and its evenness. The roller also has to be charged with a consistent film each time, because the drawing itself must be kept free of ink while the blank stone takes it.

questions.explanation: The ink sits as a surface film that the paper lifts away, so each pull needs a fresh, evenly charged roller. Reusing the first coat would give a thinner, patchier second impression.
questions.hint: Each pull takes ink off the surface.

questions.hint: Divide the image area by the sheet area.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A print and its plate set side by side
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a print and its plate are mounted together.
questions.stem: A curator's file note asks why a curator mounts a print and its plate together rather than showing the print alone.

answer.exemplar: Showing the plate beside the impression lets the viewer read two documents at once: the finished image and the evidence of how it was made. The matrix exposes the cut line, the file marks, the sequence of corrections and the wear that has accumulated with each pull, none of which survive in the impression itself. Placed together, the two objects also make clear how a printing matrix produces its image, and how many impressions a plate can bear before its line is lost.

questions.explanation: The plate exposes the cut line, tool marks, corrections and wear that the impression cannot show, so mounting the two lets the viewer read the finished image and its making at once.
questions.hint: The plate is the evidence of making.

questions.hint: Multiply the ink per pull by the number of pulls.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An installation represented by crates and photographs
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dispersed installation remains an object of continuing obligation.
questions.stem: A dispute file note asks why an installation documented in crates and photographs is treated in a claims dispute as an object of continuing obligation.

answer.exemplar: An installation is not a single thing that can be pointed at; it is an arrangement of components, a site, a scale and a set of relationships between them. When the crates are separated and the site built over, that arrangement survives only as a record in the paperwork and the photographs, and the record carries obligations of care, attribution and return that a conserved object does not. The duty therefore attaches to the components and the documentation together, which is why a file of this kind is treated as a living obligation rather than a closed inventory.

questions.explanation: An installation is an arrangement of components and a site rather than a single object, so once those are separated the record carries the duties of care, attribution and return. The file remains an obligation.
questions.hint: The arrangement outlives the crates.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why even press pressure matters for a lithographic pull.

stimulus.body: The press record reads: the stone was inked with a roller in one direction, the sheet was laid on the dampened surface, and the platen was lowered with even pressure across the whole sheet.

questions.stem: From the press record, a legal clerk explains why even pressure across the whole sheet matters.

options.text: Even pressure is needed so the paper does not tear, since the stone is very hard
options.misconception: gives a reason about tearing rather than printing

options.text: The pull must touch the whole inked area evenly, or parts of the image print lighter or darker
Even pressure keeps the stone from cracking under the weight of the press bed

options.misconception: misattributes the adhesion of ink to pressure

questions.explanation: The impression transfers the ink film through contact, so any area the platen does not reach receives less pressure and prints lighter than its neighbours. Even contact is what makes the tone across the sheet uniform.

questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Read the grain and size of a wood block as constraints on a carving.
questions.stem: A clerk's file note describes a pear-wood block measuring 20 by 30 centimetres with its grain running vertically.

options.text: The grain is irrelevant, because any block can be cut in any direction without harm
options.misconception: believes wood can be cut across the grain without risk

options.text: The carver must orient the image to the grain, since cutting across it risks splitting the block
The block is too small for the planned image, so the image must be reduced in scale
options.misconception: jumps to a size problem with no dimensions given

options.text: The vertical grain shows the block is composite, so the carver must avoid the joins
options.misconception: reads grain direction as evidence of construction

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a relief is composed for one viewpoint.
questions.stem: A file note asks why a relief carving cannot be viewed properly from the side, while a figure carved in the round can.

answer.exemplar: A relief shares its block with the background that stays standing behind it, so the whole mass of the carving is at risk of being seen from an angle, and from the side the figure collapses into a thin edge with the ground pressed against it. The composition was planned for a frontal view, where the depth of cut reads as gradations of light and shadow across a single surface. A figure carved in the round has no such constraint, because each side was carved to be finished.

questions.explanation: A relief is composed for a frontal view, where its cut depths read as tones, while from the side the figure collapses into a thin edge against its ground. A round carving is finished on every side.
questions.hint: Relief is built for one viewpoint.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: Explain why direct carving is described as a dialogue with the material.
questions.stem: A file note asks why direct carving is described as a dialogue with the material rather than the execution of a design.

answer.exemplar: A design drawn on paper assumes a block of any size, any grain and any hardness, but wood is none of those things at once. As the waste is cleared, the carver meets knots, resin lines and changes of grain that dictate how the tool travels and where it may not cut, and the image must be adjusted to what the material permits. The result is neither the drawing nor a mere copy of the block, but an image found through working within those limits, which is why the process is described as a dialogue.

questions.explanation: A drawing assumes any block, but the carver meets grain, knots and resin that dictate how the tool travels, so the image must be adjusted to what the material allows. The result is a negotiation.
questions.hint: The material answers back.

questions.topic: An enclosed path ending at a plain wall
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an enclosed path is not simply an empty gallery.

answer.exemplar: An empty gallery has nothing for the visitor to do but look at nothing, whereas a passage has a sequence, a duration and an ending that the visitor supplies physically by walking. The turns withhold what lies ahead, and the bare wall receives the attention that the route has been building. The work therefore consists of the visitor's own movement and the moment of stopping, and it would disappear entirely if the route were removed or the wall filled with other work.

questions.explanation: A passage has sequence, duration and an ending that the visitor supplies by walking, and the bare wall receives the attention the route has been building. Without the route, the wall would be an empty surface.
questions.hint: The route makes the wall mean something.

questions.topic: A single-ink poster with a large image
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one-ink posters differ between printing processes.
questions.stem: A print room note asks why a single-ink poster could be produced by several different printing processes without looking quite the same.

answer.exemplar: A single ink limits the palette but says nothing about the surface that carries it. Relief printing gives crisp edges and any tone built from visible lines or dots, lithography can hold a continuous and velvety black, and screen printing lays a flat film of ink that often shows the texture of the mesh. Each process also changes the weight of the ink and the way it sits on the paper, so the same image reads differently in the hand. The process, not the ink, produces the character of the poster.

questions.explanation: One ink fixes the palette but not the surface: relief gives crisp edges, lithography a velvety continuous black, screen printing a flat film showing its mesh. Each lays the ink differently on the paper.
questions.hint: The ink is the same; the surface is not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ink rolled across a drawn stone
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the ink film must be of consistent thickness.
questions.stem: A press room note asks why the ink film on a lithographic stone must be of consistent thickness across the whole surface.

answer.exemplar: Each area of a lithographic stone receives ink from the roller, and the amount of ink held at each point is what becomes the darkness of that point on the paper. If the film is thicker in one region than another, the pull will print one passage darker than its neighbour, and the drawing's carefully graded tones will be broken. Because ink is oily and does not soak in, the surface must also be wiped clean between impressions, so that stray ink from the last pull does not print.

questions.explanation: The thickness of the ink film at each point sets the darkness printed there, so an uneven film breaks the drawing's graded tones and prints one passage darker. Ink that has not soaked in must be wiped away.
questions.hint: Uneven film prints uneven tone.

questions.stem: A gallery note asks why an impression pulled from a copper plate looks cleaner than the plate it came from.

answer.exemplar: The impression records only the ink that was actually transferred, and the matrix is cleaned, inked and wiped before every pull so that surplus ink and debris do not print. What remains on the plate is the working surface itself: the cut line, its burr, the file marks left by the burin and any corrections the artist made after pulling a proof. questions.explanation: Each pull transfers only the ink in the cut lines, so the impression is a cleaned and filtered version of the matrix, while the plate keeps its cut line, burr, file marks and corrections.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An installation represented by crates and photographs
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a photographic record cannot stand as the work itself.
questions.stem: A custody file note asks why an installation's photographic record alone cannot be treated as the work itself.

answer.exemplar: The photographs fix the installation's appearance at the moment of documentation, and that appearance depends on a site, a scale, a light and a set of relations between components that only exist when they are together. A record of the whole cannot be assembled from separate records of parts, and it cannot show how the work behaves in time, underfoot or in the dark. The components in their crates therefore remain the primary evidence, with the photographs as the account of how they were meant to stand.

questions.explanation: A photograph fixes one appearance in one place and cannot show the condition, weight or construction of the parts, nor how the work behaves in time. The components remain the primary evidence.
questions.hint: Photographs hold one moment, not the work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A print and its plate set side by side
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the acceptable impressions in a limited edition after spoilage.
questions.stem: A file note records that a plate's edition was fixed at 30 impressions, of which 4 were spoiled before completion. How many acceptable impressions does the edition yield?
questions.explanation: The edition limit is 30 impressions and 4 of them were spoiled, so 30 minus 4 leaves 26 acceptable impressions. The plate can then be retired or its limit renegotiated.
questions.hint: Subtract the spoiled pulls from the limit.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ink rolled across a drawn stone
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a stone must be wiped between impressions.

stimulus.body: The press note records: the stone was inked, the sheet pulled, and the bed opened again so that the stone could be wiped and re-inked before the next sheet was laid.

questions.stem: From the press note, a legal clerk explains why the stone is wiped between impressions.

options.text: Because the paper needs a damp surface to soak up the ink as it is pressed
options.misconception: describes the stone as dampening the paper

options.text: Because the stone must be kept warm, and wiping is how the heat is taken away
options.misconception: confuses wiping with cooling the stone

options.text: Because surplus ink left on the stone would print in the next impression and dirty the image
Because the drawing must be re-inked each time to keep the greasy lines clear
options.misconception: reverses which part of the image is grease and which is ink

questions.explanation: The stone carries a film of ink across its whole surface, and the drawing repels it only where the grease is. If that film were not wiped away, the next pull would print the previous sheet's ink as a dirty veil.
questions.hint: Leftover ink prints as dirt.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A single-ink poster with a large image
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a single ink makes possible and what it forbids.
questions.stem: Two closing questions from the file on a single-ink poster: first, what the one ink makes possible; second, what it forbids.

options.text: First, the extension of the sheet beyond its paper size; second, the use of halftone dots
options.misconception: misreads what a second impression or dots would do

options.text: First, a complete range of colours in the shadows; second, the printing of any text at all
options.misconception: believes one ink can render a coloured range

options.text: First, the reproduction of a photograph in continuous tone; second, the use of a second impression
options.misconception: credits one ink with continuous photographic tone

options.text: First, a hard contrast between ink and bare paper; second, any graded colour or subtle tone

questions.explanation: With one ink, the sheet divides sharply into printed and unprinted, so a bold image and clear type can be built with great clarity. What the ink cannot do is produce graded colour or continuous tone.
questions.hint: One ink divides the sheet into two values.
